name: RED, USE and the Golden Signals
intent: Know which few signals to look at first, and in what order, so a failing system is diagnosed in minutes instead of by scrolling through hundreds of graphs.
scenario: At 20:10 the checkout page becomes slow. The service has four dependencies and a database behind a connection pool, and the dashboard has 200 graphs. Which three do you open first, and what does each one rule out?
problem: A request-driven system can be slow or broken in a dozen ways: too much traffic, a bad deploy, a slow dependency, a lock in the database, an exhausted connection pool, a memory leak. Each leaves a different fingerprint, but only if you looked at the right signal. An average latency graph says 'slower' and nothing else, and it can even improve while the service is failing, because fast errors pull it down. Without a short, ordered checklist, on-call engineers guess, and guessing is slow.

howItWorks.title: Golden signals: four questions about any service
howItWorks.text: Google's SRE book names four: latency (how long requests take), traffic (how much demand), errors (how many requests fail) and saturation (how full the scarcest resource is). They are deliberately generic, so the same four graphs are the first thing you open for a web tier, a queue consumer or a database. Latency of failed requests must be tracked apart from successful ones: a 500 returned in 5 ms and a timeout after 3 s both count as errors, but mixing them into one latency curve hides both.

howItWorks.title: RED: the view from the request, per service and per endpoint
howItWorks.text: RED (Tom Wilkie) is the golden signals minus saturation, for services that handle requests: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second or as a share of rate) and Duration (a distribution, so p50 and p99, never only the mean). Record it for every endpoint and for every outbound dependency call. A checkout that is slow while the payments call is normal and the database call is normal points at checkout's own code or resources; a slow payments call points at payments. RED answers 'who is hurting users, and which hop is slow'.

howItWorks.title: USE: the view from the resource, per CPU, memory, disk, network and pool
howItWorks.text: USE (Brendan Gregg) is for resources, anything with a capacity: Utilization (percent of time busy, or of capacity used), Saturation (work that is waiting: CPU run queue, disk queue, threads blocked on a connection pool, pending accepts) and Errors (resource-level: dropped packets, disk errors, pool timeouts). Utilization says 'busy'; saturation says 'queueing, so latency is already being added'. Saturation is the leading indicator: queue depth climbs before latency and errors do, because requests spend time in line before anything times out.

howItWorks.title: Combine them: RED finds the hop, USE finds the reason
howItWorks.text: Walk top-down. Is the user-facing latency or error budget burning (see SLOs)? Then RED on the service: is it traffic (rate up), errors (a deploy), or duration? Then RED on each dependency to find the slow hop. Then USE on the resources of that hop: a saturated connection pool with an idle database CPU means threads are waiting on locks or on a leaked connection, not on capacity. Finally open traces and logs for that one component. Each step removes most of the search space.

howItWorks.title: Know what each method cannot see
howItWorks.text: RED misses a resource that is filling up quietly, such as a heap climbing toward a GC death spiral, until duration finally moves. USE misses anything that is not a resource: a bad deploy that returns 500 quickly leaves CPU, memory, pools and disks looking perfectly healthy. Neither tells a leaked pool connection from a long lock wait unless you also record the duration of the database call itself. That is why you want both views on one dashboard, with the same time axis.

howItWorks.title: Build the dashboard as a story, not a wall
howItWorks.text: Top row: the SLO and the golden signals for the user-facing service. Second row: RED per dependency. Third row: USE for the few resources that matter (host CPU and run queue, memory and GC, each connection pool, the database). Link each row to the logs and traces for the same time range. A panel earns its place if someone has used it to decide something; 'total requests ever' counters, 40 near-identical CPU graphs, and graphs with no baseline are vanity.

pros: A short, memorable checklist: three signals per service and three per resource, so a tired on-call engineer follows it at 3 a.m.
Generic: the same layout works for every service, which makes dashboards consistent and easy to template
Splits the search in two: RED localises the service or hop, USE explains why, so you rarely need to read code first
Saturation gives early warning, before users see slow responses or errors
Cheap: a counter, a histogram and a handful of gauges per service cover almost all of it
cons: Neither method covers correctness or business outcomes (wrong totals, missing emails); they show health, not truth
Per-endpoint and per-dependency breakdowns multiply the number of time series, so label choices matter (see cardinality)
Saturation is the hardest signal to define: the right queue or limit differs per resource and is often not exported by default
A symptom-first dashboard can mislead when a slow dependency is itself a symptom of something upstream, so treat the result as a hypothesis to confirm in traces
whenToUse: Any request-driven service: start with RED per endpoint plus RED on each outbound call
Any shared resource with finite capacity (hosts, connection pools, thread pools, queues, disks, network links): USE
Building the first on-call dashboard for a new service, or cleaning up one that grew to hundreds of panels
Incident triage, as the fixed order of questions before anyone opens a log search
whenNotToUse: As the only monitoring for batch and streaming jobs, where the useful signals are freshness, backlog and throughput rather than request duration
As a substitute for business and correctness checks: a perfect RED dashboard can sit above a service that returns wrong answers
For one-off scripts or tiny internal tools where a log line and a restart is cheaper than any dashboard
To derive alerts from every panel: page on user-facing symptoms and keep most USE graphs as diagnosis aids
pitfalls: Showing only the mean latency: it hides the tail (a few seconds-long requests barely move it) and even falls during an incident that returns fast errors
Mixing failed and successful requests in one duration histogram: fast 5xx responses make the service look quicker, and slow timeouts hide among the slowest successes
Reading utilization as saturation: 100% busy with an empty queue is healthy; 60% CPU averaged over a minute can hide a per-core run queue and bursts that queue requests
Averaging a metric across the fleet, so one hot host or one bad endpoint disappears into the mean; keep per-instance and per-endpoint views
Omitting the connection pool from USE: pool wait time rarely shows up on host CPU or memory graphs, yet it is one of the most common causes of slow requests
Counting RED errors only as HTTP 5xx and missing timeouts, client disconnects, and 200 responses that carry an error body
Dashboards without baselines or previous-day overlays, so nobody can tell whether 40% is normal for a Friday evening

roles.label: Dashboard
roles.description: The few panels read top-down: SLO, then RED, then USE, then logs and traces.

roles.label: Checkout service
roles.description: The user-facing service whose Rate, Errors and Duration are recorded per endpoint.

roles.label: Downstream service
roles.description: A service the checkout calls; its Duration is recorded on every outbound call.

roles.label: Connection pool
roles.description: A resource with finite capacity: Utilization is connections in use, Saturation is threads waiting for one.

roles.label: Database
roles.description: The data store behind the pool; its query duration and host USE show whether it is slow or merely waited on.

quiz.question: Checkout latency p99 jumped from 300 ms to 4 s at 20:10. Request rate and error rate are flat, and the payments call is normal, but checkout's database call p99 is 10 times higher. What is the best next step?
options: Add more checkout instances to absorb the load
Open USE signals for the database and its pool
Roll back the last checkout deploy to be safe
Check the fleet-wide average latency graph
quiz.explanation: RED has already narrowed the problem to the database hop, so the next question is why: utilisation, saturation and errors of the resources behind it, including pool wait. Flat traffic means more instances will not help. The average latency graph adds nothing the p99 does not already show.

quiz.question: During an incident, users report failures and slow pages, but the dashboard shows mean latency falling from 180 ms to 130 ms. Error rate rose from 0.1% to 30%. What explains the graph?
options: The slow requests were cached, which lowered the mean
Traffic fell, so the servers had less work
Latency is measured at the wrong percentile
Fast error responses are pulling the mean down
quiz.explanation: Failed requests that return in a few milliseconds are averaged in with the successful ones, so the mean improves while the service fails. Track errors as their own signal and keep the duration of failures apart from successes, using percentiles rather than the mean.

quiz.question: A service runs on 20 instances. Users complain of 8 s responses, but the fleet-wide p99 and CPU averages look only slightly worse than usual. What is the most likely gap in the dashboard?
options: No per-instance view, so a bad host is averaged away
No error budget panel on the service dashboard
Too few CPU graphs shown for each host
Latency charts use a one-minute window only
quiz.explanation: A single host with a long run queue contributes a small share of requests, so fleet-wide aggregates hide it. Keeping per-instance and per-endpoint breakdowns shows the outlier at once. A budget panel or a narrower window would not reveal which host is hurting users.
